abstract.p: Bioactive peptides are beneficial or have physiological effects on the life activities of biological organisms. The functions of bioactive peptides are diverse, usually with one or more, so accurately detecting the multiple functions of multi-functional peptides is extremely important. Traditional experimental identification methods are time-consuming, laborious and costly. To overcome these problems, we adopt a computational biology approach and propose a new model BPFun based on deep learning, which can predict seven functions including anticancer, antibacterial, antihypertensive and so on. In BPFun, we obtained the features of bioactive peptides from different aspects, including biological and physicochemical features. Meanwhile, adopting data augmentation to solve the problem of data imbalance. We combine convolutional networks of different scales and Bi-LSTM layers to obtain high-level feature vectors of different features. Finally, the prediction performance is improved by combining these fused features and combining the self-attention mechanism and the Bi-LSTM layer. Our experiments show that BPFun based on five types of sequence features significantly improves the prediction performance of bioactive peptides. Experiments on the test dataset showed that BPFun gets the accuracy and absolute truth value of 0.6577 and 0.6573 on the dataset of seven functional classifications and was superior to other methods. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/291357657/BPFun.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Bioactive peptides are usually small molecular peptides [1], which are a class of peptides with multiple biological functions and widely exist in animals, plants and foods [2]. As bioactive peptides play an important role in regulating various functions of the body, peptide drugs also have the characteristics of significant curative effect, short half-life and low toxicity [3]. In recent years, more and more bioactive peptides with different functions have been found [4–6]. At the same time, more and more experimental data show that many bioactive peptides have multiple functions. For example, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) can protect the host from pathogen invasion [7], while some AMPs also have other functions, such as antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral and anticancer [8]. Antiangiogenic peptides (AAPs) are used in the field of cancer treatment because of their function of reducing or inhibiting angiogenesis [5, 9], and they also play an important role in the treatment of other angiogenesis-dependent diseases [10–12]. Some antioxidant peptides (AOPs) extracted from natural proteins may contain additional bioactive properties, such as cholesterol-lowering or antimicrobial properties, in addition to their own antioxidant functions [3, 13]. Accurately predicting the functional activity of bioactive peptides has various meanings: (1) it helps to study the mechanism of action of existing bioactive peptides; (2) it helps to discover new bioactive peptides and to search for bioactive peptides with specific functions; and (3) it helps to develop new peptide drugs to meet the needs of health and safety.

Because bioactive peptides have a wide range of application prospects, it is particularly important to realize the method of large-scale identification of bioactive peptides. Traditional experimental methods cannot meet the needs of peptide function identification, and the accurate identification of bioactive peptides by computational methods has become more and more important. There are quite a few existing methods that can be used to identify bioactive peptides. In 2023, Lee et al. [14] proposed antibacterial peptide function prediction based on the Bert model, named AMP-BERT, which has a bidirectional encoder representation (BERT) architecture from the transformer [15]. In 2022, Pang et al. [16] proposed a method combining transformer neural network architecture and natural language processing knowledge to identify AMP and AMP's functional activity. In 2023, Xu et al. [17] proposed a framework of iAMPCN based on deep learning. The model is mainly based on four types of sequence features and can predict AMP and its functional activity. In 2021, Chen et al. [18] proposed to improve the prediction ability of anti-cancer peptides (ACPs) by using a data augmentation method, called ACP-DA, which could improve the prediction performance of the model while solving the problem of insufficient sample size. In 2022, Bhattarai et al. [19] improved the features used based on Chen [18] to further improve the accuracy of predicting ACPs. In 2019, Zahiri et al. [20] proposed AntAngioCOOL to predict AAPs. They extracted useful description information from different aspects such as PseAAC, atomic spectra and physicochemical spectra to build models. Additionally, another methods [21–24] are usually only applicable to the functional identification of a single bioactive peptide, and only two methods can perform multi-functional identification of bioactive peptides related to the human. One is a deep learning method called MLBP proposed by Tang et al. [25] in 2022 based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) [26] and gated recurrent units (GRU) [27], and the other is a multi-activity prediction method, called MPMABP, for bioactive peptides based on CNN and Bi-LSTM [28] proposed by Li et al. [29] in 2022. Compared to MLBP, MPMABP has been improved by constructing a residual network to ensure that the information of peptides is not lost and replacing GRU with LSTM. However, MPMABP used the same dataset as MLBP, where the variety of bioactive peptides did not increase and did not solve the problem of data imbalance.

The identification of bioactive peptides with multiple functions is a multi-label classification problem, so multi-label classification methods from text, image, and bioinformatics fields over the past few decades can also be used to identify bioactive peptides [30–36]. In 2008, a multi-label learning method, named CLR, proposed by Johannes et al. [33] introduced an artificial calibration label, which is a method that combines paired preference learning with traditional correlation classification techniques. In 2018, a novel cost-sensitive multi-label learning model, named CPNL, with positive and negative label pair correlation proposed by Wu et al. [31] solves the problem that binary correlation (BR) ignores label correlation. In 2020, another method combining ranking support vector machine and binary correlation with robust low-rank learning, named RBRL, proposed by Wu et al. [34] inherits the ranking loss minimization advantage of ranking support vector machine (Rank-SVM) and overcomes the problem of BR class imbalance and ignoring the problem of label correlation. In 2019, the multi-label deep forest method, named MLDF, proposed by Zhou et al. [35] includes two important parts: measuring perceptual feature reuse and measuring perceptual layer growth. In 2007, Grigorios et al. [36] proposed a multi-label classification method called RAKEL that uses a single-label classifier to consider label correlation.

However, among the multiple methods mentioned above, the multi-label classification method that can be applied to multiple tasks has limited predictive power when used alone for the task of multi-functional identification of bioactive peptides, and the accuracy of identification is also affected by zero-padding of peptide sequences, which cannot provide comprehensive and accurate functional identification. MLBP and MPMABP use peptide sequences as the only input information, and their accuracy decreases significantly when faced with the identification of more categories of peptide functions.

Given these limitations, we propose a new method BPFun for identifying bioactive peptides. For feature construction, we extracted features from multiple perspectives to capture the relationship between peptide sequence information and function. We selected five different feature representation methods as inputs: peptide sequence, peptide sequence encoded by one-hot, peptide sequence encoded by AAindex1 [37], and peptide sequence features obtained using pre-trained models ProtT5 [38] and ESM-2 [39]. The construction process of the BPFun model can be summarized as follows: (1) Obtain and organize a dataset of bioactive peptides and preprocess it, which includes seven bioactive peptides: AMP, ACP, ADP, AHP, AIP, AAP, and AOP; (2) Using AAindex1 and pre-trained models ProtT5 and ESM-2 to process peptide sequences to obtain new encoding and features; (3) Replace the amino acid letters in the peptide sequence with natural numbers to obtain the preprocessed peptide sequence and use one-hot encoding; (4) Using deep learning models to construct BPFun models; (5) Evaluate the performance of the model. Use nine metrics to evaluate the performance of BPFun. Finally, the performance evaluation structure indicates that under the combined action of these five different features, we have effectively improved the representation of peptide sequences. Compared with existing prediction tools, our BPFun has excellent performance in identifying multi-functional peptides and outperforms MLBP and MPMABP in the results of seven functional classifications.

sec.title: Data
sec.p:
Based on the principle of being able to identify more bioactive peptides, we used nine bioactive peptides related to humans retrieved from the 2020 Google Scholar engine provided by Tang et al. [25], and selected seven of them, including AMP, ACP, ADP, AHP, AIP, AAP, and AOP, with a sample size of more than 100. Among these seven bioactive peptides, the five bioactive peptides AMP, ACP, ADP, AHP, and AIP used the same experimental dataset as MLBP [25] and MPMABP [29], the AAP dataset used the same experimental dataset as AntAngioCOOL [20], and the AOP used the same dataset as AnOxPePred [40]. These datasets were screened using the clustering tool CD-HIT [41] with a threshold set to 0.9. Because there are a large number of sequences with 2–4 amino acids in the AOP dataset, we uniformly processed all data and selected peptide sequences with at least 5 amino acids. We finally obtained 2,409 AMPs, 646 ACPs, 514 ADPs, 868 AHPs, 1,678 AIPs, 134 AAPs, and 318 AOPs. We randomly selected 20% of the dataset as the test dataset and used the remaining 80% as the training dataset. The details of the training and test datasets are shown in Table 1. Apart from single functional bioactive peptides, there are a total of 154 bioactive peptides with two types of functional activity, and there are no bioactive peptides with more functions. Among them, 92 bioactive peptides belong to AMP and ACP; 1 bioactive peptide belongs to ACP and AHP; 2 bioactive peptides belong to ACP and AOP; 4 bioactive peptides belong to ACP and AAP; 22 bioactive peptides belong to ADP and AIP; 14 bioactive peptides belong to ADP and AHP; 3 bioactive peptides belong to AMP and AOP; 2 bioactive peptides belong to ADP and AOP; and 14 bioactive peptides belong to AOP and AHP.Table 1

sec.title: Data augmentation
sec.p: Due to the imbalance in the quantity of data among different categories, we have adopted a data augmentation approach to increase categories with insufficient data volume. Its basic principle is similar to masking technology, mainly to enhance the range of information in the sequence, and to enhance the generalization ability of the model by simulating information loss. When amino acids are masked, the masked value is uncertain, which increases the range of representation information of the sequence, while only replacing one amino acid to maintain the locality of the sequence without being destroyed. We use a specific character to randomly replace an amino acid in the sequence, and the processed sequence is considered a new sequence, belonging to the same category as the original sequence. It is worth noting that our data augmentation operation is only performed on the training dataset, and no changes will be made to the test dataset. The added data is placed after the original data by category. Finally, we obtained the results shown in Table 1, excluding duplicate sequences.

sec.title: Feature
sec.p: In the experiment, we used five different types of encoding methods to represent peptide sequences. To ensure the efficiency of our process of obtaining these five sequence representations, we analyzed the length distribution of all data. In the results of length distribution, 99.3% of the sequence length was less than 128, 92.1% of the sequence length was less than 64, and 79% of the sequence length was less than 32. Therefore, we selected the peptide sequence length range from 5 to 32. Sequences with a length less than 5 will be deleted, sequences with a length greater than 32 will be truncated from the first 32 amino acids, and sequences with a length less than 32 will be filled using the zero-padding method, to ensure that there is sufficient sequence information without filling in too many zeros, which will affect data quality. Finally, the data as shown in Table 1 was obtained.

The resulting data is then encoded or extracted using five independent parts (lines 6–25). Finally, use the obtained sequence information to train the model (lines 27–34).

Our model is roughly divided into four parts: the first part is the input, which is used to input the sequence of bioactive peptides; the second part is the deep learning module, which is mainly used to process and learn five different input information and pass it down; the third part mainly integrates the feature vectors passed from the upper layer and improves the performance of the model through self-attention mechanism; the last part uses sigmoid as the activation function of the classification module to output the results. sec.title: Evaluation metrics
sec.p: TP, TN, FP, and FN represent true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, respectively.

sec.title: Distribution of amino acids
sec.p:
To analyze the distribution of amino acids in the sequence, we used weblogo [50] to generate sequence logos. The residues appearing at each position in the sequence are drawn graphically, and the cumulative residues at each position can reflect the consistency of residues at that position. The size of the graphical character corresponding to a residue is proportional to the frequency of the residue at that position. Because entropy values are designed during the calculation process, if the sequence letters in a column are more chaotic, the entropy value will be larger, and the letters will be shorter; conversely, if there is more regularity, the entropy value will be smaller, and the letters will be taller. The amino acid graphics for each multi-functional peptide are shown in Fig. 3. Among these seven bioactive peptides, there is no position where a certain amino acid is always present, and most positions have multiple amino acids that can be substituted. In ACP, alanine (A), glycine (G), lysine (K), and leucine (L) are predominant, and the first amino acid usually appears in alanine, glycine, lysine, and phenylalanine (F); in ADP, alanine, leucine, and valine (V) are predominant; in AHP, proline (P) is predominant; in AIP, alanine and leucine are predominant; in AOP, leucine and proline are usually predominant, and the 23-th amino acid in the sequence is usually cysteine or leucine or tyrosine (Y); in AAP, cysteine, glycine, arginine, and serine are predominant; AMP is dominated by glycine and lysine. In general, these seven bioactive peptides do not have a certain amino acid fragment that always appears, and there are one or more amino acids that can be substituted at each position.Fig. 3
The distribution of the first 32 amino acids of seven different bioactive peptides

sec.title: Different lengths of sequences
sec.p:
We chose to set the length of the sequence used in the experiment to 32 based on the fact that 79% of the data had a length less than 32. As shown in Table 3, we trained on different lengths. When the sequence length was 256 residues, the accuracy of these seven bioactive peptides was 0.634, while when there were only 32 residues, the accuracy was 0.649, with a difference of about 2%. The overall trend is towards a slight increase in accuracy as the length of the sequence decreases. The other metrics also reflect this trend. And we also analyzed the time spent processing a piece of data when using different lengths, as shown in Table 4. For the length of a sequence, longer sequences require longer processing time, especially when using the pre-trained model ProtT5 to extract sequence features, which takes a lot of time. In this experiment, reducing the length of the sequence used to a certain extent can almost ignore the impact on the experimental results, but it can save a lot of time for the entire experimental process. We believe that reducing the sequence length appropriately will not affect the experimental results, but can greatly reduce time consumption during the experiment. Therefore, in this experiment, we selected the first 32 residues of the truncated sequence and filled in a small amount of zeros when insufficient.Table 3

sec.title: Different numbers of sequences
sec.p:
When increasing the number of datasets, considering the different types of bioactive peptides with varying quantities, we chose to start with 500 and increase each time, up to 2500, to test whether different quantities have an impact on the performance of the BPFun model. Firstly, to ensure that the original dataset is used, no processing will be performed when the number of bioactive peptides exceeds the value we have selected. Subsequently, increase the quantity of bioactive peptides that are less than the selected value until the selected quantity is reached. As shown in Table 5, the metrics vary for different quantities of bioactive peptides. In terms of Precision alone, the more bioactive peptides there are between 500 and 2000, the higher the Precision. When the number of bioactive peptides is 2500, Precision will decrease. The other metrics have similar patterns of change. Overall, the performance of the model is best when the number of each bioactive peptide is controlled in 2000.Table 5

sec.title: Classification comparison of different features
sec.p:
In addition to the impact of different lengths on the research, we also analyzed the impact of different encoding methods or feature extraction methods on the features of different bioactive peptides. All sequences have a length of 32, and we encode them using three encoding methods: the number sequence converted from the original sequence, one-hot, and AAindex1; ProtT5 and ESM-2 pre-trained models extract preliminary features. Subsequently, we input these five features into the decision tree classifier. The average data from multiple experiments and the results obtained for the given model are shown in Fig. 4, the feature representations obtained using one-hot encoding and ESM-2 pre-training model can improve the predictive performance of these seven bioactive peptides, with higher ACC values compared to others; AAPs and AOPs have achieved good results in encoding and feature extraction using these five methods. We tested the impact of features obtained through different methods on our model using different combinations, and the results are shown in Table S1. Among them, two features obtained by pre-trained model contribute more to our model, while the other three features play an important role in improving the model performance.Fig. 4
Heat map visualization of decision tree classifier results based on different features

sec.title: Feature visualization
sec.p: In the experiment, we combined sequence information, One-hot and AAindex1 encoding information, and feature information extracted using pre-trained models ProtT5 and ESM-2 to represent peptides. To verify that all five types of information contribute to predicting the multiple functions of peptides, we visualized the original dataset using UMAP [51] on both the training and testing datasets. Project the initial encoding vectors and high-level abstract features of all samples extracted from the model based on different input information onto a two-dimensional space.

For each type of peptide information, using the corresponding model for learning will result in better feature representations. As shown in Fig. 5, we visualized the feature information from both the training process and the independent test dataset. During the training process, using five different initial peptide sequence information alone did not effectively aggregate the same category in the results. However, when using these five different types of information simultaneously, the results were able to distinguish different categories well. On the independent test dataset, the identification ability of the five individual peptide sequence information is not up to that of the comprehensive bioactive peptide information. It can be seen that compared to using single information to identify the function of peptides, using different information from bioactive peptides can achieve better predictive ability. Therefore, this model can learn abstract representations of different bioactive peptides from the initial sequence information of peptides, information encoded using one-hot and AAindex1, and information extracted from pre-trained models ProtT5 and ESM-2, improving the ability to identify peptide functions.Fig. 5
UMAP visualization results on the dataset: A using five features individually and simultaneously on the training dataset; B using five features individually and simultaneously on the test dataset

sec.title: Comparison with other models
sec.p:
To verify the stability of BPFun, we conducted a five-fold cross-validation experiment with other multi-label classification methods. So far, MLBP and MPMABP are the latest methods for classifying multi-functional labeled bioactive peptides. MLBP utilizes a deep learning method that combines CNN and Bi-GRU; MPMABP constructed a residual network based on MLBP and replaced GRU with LSTM. At the same time, we have also chosen other multi-label algorithms that can be used to predict bioactive peptides, such as sorted support vector machines and binary correlation with robust low-rank learning (RBRL), which inherit the ranking loss minimization advantage of rank support vector machine (Rank-SVM) and overcomes the problem of BR class imbalance and ignoring the problem of label correlation; multi-label learning with deep forest (MLDF), which utilizes measurement perceptual feature reuse and measurement perceptual layer growth; calibrated label sorting (CLR) combines pairwise preference learning with traditional correlation classification techniques; random k-label set (RAKEL), considering label correlation by using a single label classifier. We use the five-fold stratified cross validation on the training dataset. To avoid overfitting during the five-fold cross-validation experiment on the expanded training dataset, which may lead to biased experimental results, we chose to experiment on the original training dataset. As shown in Table 6, BPFun outperforms the above methods in eight aspects: Precision, Coverage, Accuracy, F1 value, Absolute true, Absolute false, Sen, and MCC. Compared with other method, BPFun has improved Precision by 0.022–0.178, Coverage by 0.02–0.179, Accuracy by 0.022–0.178, F1 value by 0.021–0.179, Absolute true by 0.024–0.178, and Absolute false by 0.008–0.036. The deviation of Precision, Coverage, Accuracy, F1 value and Absolute true is maintained at 0.011, and the deviation of Absolute false is maintained at 0.002. The results indicate that our model has an excellent performance in identifying multi-functional peptides, while also exhibiting certain stability.Table 6

To verify the performance of the model on an independent test dataset, we used the expanded training dataset for training. In the end, our method outperformed other methods among the eight metrics. As shown in Table 7, our method BPFun still achieved the best results on our dataset containing seven types of multi-functional peptides. Precision increased by 0.0376–0.1378, Coverage increased by 0.0359–0.1187, Accuracy increased by 0.0376–0.1378, F1 value increased by 0.0367–0.1193, Absolute true increased by 0.0391–0.1211, and Absolute false decreased by 0.0032–0.0287. The general multi-label classification methods RBRL, MLDF, CLR, and RAKEL have slight limitations in their ability to specifically predict multiple functions of bioactive peptides. MPMABP performs well in predicting five types of multi-functional peptides but performs poorly in predicting seven types of multi-functional peptides. The fundamental reason is that the model has multiple convolutions of different scales, which cannot effectively extract feature learning when encountering test datasets with small sample sizes. MLBP has good performance in predicting five and seven types of multi-functional peptides, but its prediction accuracy is still insufficient when only peptide sequence information is available. Further confirmation confirms that our method utilizes different feature representations to enhance the information content of peptides, making it more effective in predicting peptide functions. It also demonstrates that this method has higher complexity and stronger learning ability, providing a useful reference for predicting the detection rate of peptides from other species.Table 7

We conducted prediction results distribution for different multi-label methods and presented the relationships between sample points through UMAP. The horizontal and vertical coordinates do not represent specific biological or mathematical features, but rather represent the relative positional relationships of sample points in low dimensional space. The distance between two sample points represents their differences in the original high-dimensional data. As shown in Fig. 7. Among the six compared methods, only the prediction results of RBRL and MLDF were able to clearly distinguish different categories of bioactive peptides; the other four methods, CLR, RAKEL, MPMABP, and MLBP, can only predict a large number of categories, and in most cases, they cannot effectively distinguish the categories to which they belong. Our method BPFun achieved good results in predicting these seven different bioactive peptides, with clear boundaries between different categories and good clustering of results.Fig. 7

sec.title: Various bioactive peptides
sec.p:
To verify the predictive ability of the BPFun method for single functional bioactive peptides, we separately plotted ROC and PR curves for seven types of bioactive peptides, as shown in Fig. 8. According to the ROC curve, AMP, AHP, and AIP have higher AUC values of 0.891, 0.940, and 0.926, while the AUC values of the other four bioactive peptides are slightly lower. In the PR curve, AMP, AHP, and AIP also performed well, with higher AP values of 0.837, 0.743, and 0.762. The AP values of the other four bioactive peptides performed poorly.Fig. 8
ROC and PR curves of different types of bioactive peptides: a ROC curve; b PR curve

We also analyzed the MCC values of various methods for each class of bioactive peptides, as shown in Fig. 9. Our method BPFun performs better than the comparison method in terms of MCC values for AMP, ADP, AHP, and AIP, indicating that BPFun has better predictive ability for these four bioactive peptides than the comparison model. Our method also achieved at least moderate performance in the MCC values of ACP, AAP, and AOP, with little difference compared to the better performing methods.Fig. 9
MCC values of different multi-label methods on the test dataset of per-class bioactive peptides

We compared the sensitivity and specificity between the original dataset and the current dataset. As shown in Fig. 10. On the original dataset, the specificity of ADP, AAP, and AOP was 1, while the sensitivity was 0. This indicates that due to the imbalance of data between different categories in the original dataset, the accuracy of prediction is affected. When predicting these three types of functional peptides, the model judges most of the samples as negative samples. We alleviate the error prediction caused by data imbalance by increasing the amount of data for these less-data categories. From the results, it can be seen that the specificity of ADP, AAP, and AOP did not significantly decrease, while the sensitivity was effectively improved; the proportion of other categories in all data has decreased, and there is some fluctuation in sensitivity. From the experimental results, it can be seen that our method of expanding data can to some extent alleviate the problem of data imbalance between multiple categories of data. We alleviate the erroneous predictions caused by data imbalance by increasing the amount of data for these categories with less data. The originally insufficient data has been expanded to expand the representation range of the dataset. Most enhancement techniques involve constructing similar objects, which can result in similar sequences, which is a common problem in data augmentation techniques. However, some datasets are too small, making it difficult for the model to pay attention to the representation range of this type of data. By using enhanced methods to expand the representation range of this type of data, the problem of limited data volume has been improved to some extent. Therefore, although there may be overfitting for learning single category data, this overfitting is within a reasonable range and will not expand to other categories. From the results, it can be seen that the specificity of ADP, AAP, and AOP did not significantly decrease, while the sensitivity was effectively improved; the proportion of other categories in all data has decreased, and there is some fluctuation in sensitivity, but the change is small. From the experimental results, it can be seen that our method of expanding data can to some extent alleviate the problem of data imbalance between multiple categories of data.Fig. 10

The final results showed that our method BPFun outperformed other methods in predicting multi-functional bioactive peptides. Our method BPFun can predict the activity of the vast majority of bioactive peptides, but there are shortcomings in predicting antioxidant peptide AOP. On the contrary, the MLBP method performs well in predicting AOP, but its overall performance is not as good as our method in the selected bioactive peptide sequences; The MPMABP method has insufficient ability in predicting the activity of seven bioactive peptides. From the prediction results of the above examples, our method BPFun is superior to existing methods in predicting multi-functional bioactive peptides.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Due to the scarcity of bioactive peptides that can determine their functional activity, and the irregular composition of amino acids, accurately predicting the functional activity of bioactive peptides remains challenging. A single feature vector is not sufficient to effectively provide the demand for predicting bioactive peptides. Therefore, to improve the performance of the model in predicting bioactive peptides, we used different features to represent the same bioactive peptide, to fully utilize the information of a bioactive peptide sequence. Through visual analysis of features, it can be concluded that using the five features we have selected simultaneously is far more suitable for predicting the function of bioactive peptides than using only one feature alone. Therefore, we propose a prediction method for multi-functional bioactive peptides, called BPFun, which uses multiple feature information to predict bioactive peptides. From our experimental results, it can be seen that this method has good comprehensive performance. Compared with existing methods, BPFun has better performance in predicting bioactive peptides. We believe that the following reasons have improved the performance of BPFun.

First, we use different features to represent peptide sequences. We used five different features, including the original sequence, to describe sequence information from different perspectives. In the experiment, we made heat maps for different categories of bioactive peptides and different feature representations, and the results showed that these five different features can effectively represent the information of peptide sequences. Compared to using a single feature as input, our approach of using different features can effectively improve model performance. Among the existing methods for identifying bioactive peptides, using multiple different features can achieve more significant improvements in experiments compared to using a single feature method [18, 19].

Second, we use data augmentation to address the issue of data imbalance between different categories, especially after the number of bioactive peptide categories has increased to seven. Data augmentation is the process of generating pseudo samples by modifying the original sequence: randomly replacing a certain amino acid letter in the sequence with a specific character, and then obtaining a new sequence. The dataset obtained through data augmentation can train the model more effectively compared to the dataset without data augmentation. The model's predictive ability for categories with smaller sample sizes is significantly improved, and the sensitivity of these categories with smaller sample sizes can be significantly improved.

Finally, we optimized the model. Using convolutional layers of different scales to extract different features can effectively utilize the different features we use. The use of Bi-LSTM can effectively utilize the contextual information of peptide sequences. Meanwhile, the attention mechanism used in the model effectively improves the performance of the model. Under the same dataset conditions, our method has better performance and overall performance compared to other methods.

In summary, our proposed method BPFun has good performance in predicting the function of bioactive peptides. The different optimization methods used can effectively improve the performance of the model. Among them, using multiple different representation methods to describe sequence information and data augmentation of samples can effectively alleviate the problem of insufficient and insufficient effective information in bioactive peptide data.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Accurately identifying bioactive peptides and their functional activities is crucial for the design of functional peptides and the development of therapeutic approaches. In this work, we propose a deep neural network based BPFun for predicting the functional activity of multi-functional bioactive peptides. In this model, five different feature representation methods including sequence information were used, and the data was expanded. Then, features were extracted using CNNs of different scales, and attention mechanisms were added to process information. The prediction results of the BPFun method indicate that compared with existing bioinformatics multi-label methods and deep learning methods, the BPFun method is relatively better, or at least can supplement future computing models in this field. In the future, we will continue to study the direction of multiple feature information working together, consider more efficient feature extraction and combination methods and different algorithms, and try to select representative feature information with other feature information; we will also focus on solving the problem of data imbalance to further improve the prediction performance of multifunctional bioactive peptides. Models that use multiple different features as inputs need to consider more the range of information representation after combining different features, and deep neural networks can add more layers to improve the performance of the model. We hope that BPFun can provide effective help in predicting novel multifunctional peptides or producing peptide drugs.
